claims.text: The dynamic mechanical response of as-solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes is controlled by nanoscale Mn-based oxide precipitates.
At lower temperatures and strain rates, Mn-based oxide precipitates strengthen FeNiCrMn by impeding dislocation motion through Orowan strengthening.
At higher temperatures or lower strain rates, Mn-based oxide precipitates exert Zener drag and delay dynamic recrystallization.
As-solidified FeNiCrMn has a fine-grained microstructure.
Rapid solidification produces a uniform dispersion of nanoscale Mn-based oxide precipitates in FeNiCrMn.
An inert testing atmosphere prevents oxidation during the proposed mechanical tests.
A high density of well-dispersed Mn oxide precipitates enhances the strength of FeNiCrMn.
The precipitates support a balance of dislocation slip and twinning during deformation.
Precipitate-induced delay of dynamic recrystallization mitigates complete strain softening.
FeNiCrMn yield strength will decrease gradually with increasing temperature.
Precipitate pinning will delay full recrystallization and associated strain softening relative to material without such pinning.
Higher strain rates will produce greater yield strength than lower strain rates.
The proposed controlled study will test FeNiCrMn from 25 °C to 900 °C under uniaxial loading.
The proposed study will compare strain rates of 10^-3, 10^-2, and 10^-1 s^-1.
SEM and TEM before and after deformation will be used to assess grain size, precipitate distribution, dislocation interactions, and dynamic recrystallization.
The hypothesis is limited to rapidly cooled FeNiCrMn with a fine grain size and uniform nanoscale precipitate dispersion.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when substantial compositional segregation or dominant secondary phases are present.
Processing-dependent precipitate size, density, and interface characteristics may change strength retention and ductility.
Absence of a precipitate-associated recrystallization delay or of a correlation between precipitate distribution and mechanical trends would falsify the proposed precipitate-control mechanism.
